cards.q: Which cluster of medullary neurons generates the basic rhythm of quiet breathing?
cards.a: The pre-Botzinger complex.
options: The nucleus of the solitary tract
The pneumotaxic center
The pre-Botzinger complex
The apneustic center
cards.explanation: The pre-Botzinger complex, part of the ventral respiratory group, contains pacemaker neurons that fire in bursts and set the rhythm of eupnea. The pneumotaxic center sits in the pons and shapes the rhythm by switching inspiration off, but it does not create it. The apneustic center, also pontine, prolongs inspiration rather than timing it. The nucleus of the solitary tract houses the dorsal respiratory group, which receives sensory input and relays the drive, but the burst timing originates in the pre-Botzinger complex.

cards.q: Where is the pontine respiratory group, also called the pneumotaxic center, located?
cards.a: In the upper pons.
options: In the dorsal medulla
In the upper pons
In the lower pons
In the ventral medulla
cards.explanation: The pontine respiratory group lies in the upper pons and sends signals that limit the length of each inspiration. The lower pons is the location assigned to the apneustic center, which has the opposite effect and prolongs inspiration. The ventral medulla holds the ventral respiratory group and the pre-Botzinger complex, and the dorsal medulla holds the dorsal respiratory group, so both medullary answers name real centers in the wrong part of the brainstem.

cards.q: Which nerve carries the motor command from the medulla to the diaphragm?
cards.a: The phrenic nerve.
options: The phrenic nerve
The glossopharyngeal nerve
The vagus nerve
The intercostal nerves
cards.explanation: The phrenic nerve is the sole motor supply to the diaphragm, so the inspiratory burst reaches the main pump muscle through it. The intercostal nerves drive the external and internal intercostals, which assist but do not move the diaphragm. The vagus nerve carries mostly sensory traffic from the lungs back to the medulla, and the glossopharyngeal nerve carries carotid body afferents, so both are inputs rather than motor outputs.

cards.q: Which spinal cord segments give rise to the phrenic nerve?
cards.a: C3 to C5.
options: T1 to T4
T6 to T10
C1 to C2
C3 to C5
cards.explanation: The phrenic nerve arises from ventral rami C3, C4 and C5, which is why the old teaching phrase says C3, 4 and 5 keep the diaphragm alive. C1 to C2 is above the phrenic origin, so a lesion there cuts the pathway rather than forming it. T1 to T4 and T6 to T10 supply intercostal and abdominal muscles, which matter for forced breathing but leave the diaphragm working when they are lost.

cards.q: During quiet breathing, which group of medullary neurons carries the inspiratory drive to the spinal motor neurons?
cards.a: The dorsal respiratory group.
options: The apneustic center
The expiratory neurons of the ventral respiratory group
The dorsal respiratory group
The Botzinger complex
cards.explanation: The dorsal respiratory group fires during inspiration and projects to the phrenic and external intercostal motor neurons, so it is the output path for quiet inspiration. The expiratory neurons of the ventral respiratory group are nearly silent at rest and switch on only for forced expiration. The Botzinger complex inhibits inspiratory neurons rather than driving them, and the apneustic center is pontine, not medullary.

cards.q: Which neurons are essentially silent at rest and become active only during forced expiration?
cards.a: The expiratory neurons of the ventral respiratory group.
options: The rhythm generating neurons of the pre-Botzinger complex
The inspiratory off switch neurons of the upper pons
The inspiratory neurons of the dorsal respiratory group
The expiratory neurons of the ventral respiratory group
cards.explanation: Quiet expiration is passive, so the expiratory neurons of the ventral respiratory group stay quiet until breathing becomes forceful, when they drive the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles. The inspiratory neurons of the dorsal respiratory group and the rhythm generating neurons of the pre-Botzinger complex are both busy during ordinary quiet breathing. The off switch neurons of the upper pons are also continuously active, tuning how long each inspiration lasts rather than switching on only for effort.

cards.q: What is the stimulus for the Hering-Breuer inflation reflex?
cards.a: Stretch of airway smooth muscle at large lung volumes.
options: Irritant particles landing on the lining of the trachea
A fall in the partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli
Stretch of airway smooth muscle at large lung volumes
A rise in H+ concentration in the cerebrospinal fluid
cards.explanation: Slowly adapting stretch receptors sit in airway smooth muscle and fire when the lung is inflated, and their signal shortens inspiration so the lung is not overstretched. A fall in alveolar PO2 acts on the peripheral chemoreceptors, not on stretch receptors. A rise in cerebrospinal fluid H+ is the central chemoreceptor stimulus. Irritant particles trigger the cough and irritant reflexes, a separate protective pathway with a different receptor.

cards.q: Which nerve carries lung stretch receptor signals back to the medullary respiratory centers?
cards.a: The vagus nerve.
options: The vagus nerve
The intercostal nerves
The glossopharyngeal nerve
The phrenic nerve
cards.explanation: Vagal afferents from airway stretch receptors terminate in the dorsal respiratory group, which is why cutting both vagus nerves abolishes the Hering-Breuer reflex. The glossopharyngeal nerve carries carotid body and carotid sinus signals, a chemical and pressure pathway rather than a stretch pathway. The phrenic and intercostal nerves are motor routes to the breathing muscles, so neither returns lung volume information to the brainstem.

cards.q: A lesion destroys the pontine respiratory group but leaves the medulla intact. Predict the change in the breathing pattern.
cards.a: Inspirations become longer and deeper and the rate slows.
options: Inspirations become longer and deeper and the rate slows
Inspirations become shorter and shallower and the rate rises
Breathing stops completely because the rhythm is lost
The pattern becomes irregular but the rate and depth are unchanged
cards.explanation: The pontine respiratory group acts as an inspiratory off switch, so removing it lets each inspiration run longer, which raises tidal volume and lowers frequency. Shorter and shallower breaths would follow from too much off switch activity, the opposite of this lesion. Breathing does not stop, because the rhythm is generated in the medullary pre-Botzinger complex, which is untouched. Saying rate and depth are unchanged misses that the timing of inspiration is exactly what the pons controls.

cards.q: An opioid drug strongly inhibits neurons of the pre-Botzinger complex. Predict the immediate effect on breathing.
cards.a: Breathing frequency falls and breaths may become irregular.
options: Breathing frequency rises while tidal volume falls
Tidal volume rises with no change in frequency
Expiration becomes active while inspiration is unchanged
Breathing frequency falls and breaths may become irregular
cards.explanation: The pre-Botzinger complex sets the burst rate, so inhibiting it slows and destabilizes the rhythm, which is the classic pattern of opioid respiratory depression. A rise in frequency would require excitation of that pacemaker, not inhibition. A pure rise in tidal volume points to loss of the pontine off switch instead. Active expiration comes from recruiting the expiratory neurons of the ventral respiratory group, which inhibiting the rhythm generator does not do.

cards.q: An adult breathes quietly with a tidal volume of 450 mL, then is placed on a ventilator delivering 1500 mL breaths. When does the Hering-Breuer inflation reflex become important?
cards.a: Only during the large ventilator breaths.
options: During neither, because the reflex exists only in infants
During both, because the reflex sets every breath
Only during the quiet 450 mL breaths
Only during the large ventilator breaths
cards.explanation: In adults the stretch receptors need roughly a liter of inflation before their firing is strong enough to cut inspiration short, so the reflex guards against overinflation rather than shaping ordinary breaths. It is not what times the 450 mL resting breath, which is set by the brainstem rhythm. Saying it sets every breath overstates its role in adults. The reflex is more prominent in infants, but it is present and demonstrable in adults at large volumes, so it does not disappear after infancy.

cards.q: A patient has a complete spinal cord injury at C6. Predict the effect on the diaphragm.
cards.a: The diaphragm still works, because the phrenic roots leave above C6.
options: The diaphragm works but the medulla can no longer set its rhythm
The diaphragm is completely paralyzed on both sides
The diaphragm still works, because the phrenic roots leave above C6
The diaphragm is paralyzed on one side only
cards.explanation: The phrenic nerve arises from C3 to C5, so a lesion at C6 leaves that outflow connected to the brainstem and the diaphragm keeps contracting, although intercostal and abdominal muscles below the lesion are lost. Complete paralysis would require a lesion above C3. A one sided result would require damage to one phrenic nerve rather than a complete cord lesion. The medulla still sets the rhythm, because the descending pathway to C3 through C5 is intact.

cards.q: At the end of a quiet inspiration, the inspiratory neurons stop firing. What produces expiration?
cards.a: Elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall.
options: Elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall
A burst of firing from the pontine respiratory group to the diaphragm
Contraction of the abdominal muscles
Contraction of the internal intercostal muscles
cards.explanation: Quiet expiration is passive, so once the diaphragm relaxes the stretched elastic tissue and the surface tension of the alveoli pull the lung back down and push air out. The abdominal muscles and internal intercostals do drive expiration, but only when breathing is forced, such as during exercise or coughing. The pontine respiratory group modifies inspiratory timing and has no motor projection of its own to the diaphragm.

cards.q: A student voluntarily holds her breath during a lab exercise. Which pathway carries that command?
cards.a: Corticospinal fibers running to the respiratory motor neurons.
options: Fibers from the cortex that directly excite the pre-Botzinger complex
Sympathetic fibers from the hypothalamus to the diaphragm
Vagal fibers from the cortex to the lung stretch receptors
Corticospinal fibers running to the respiratory motor neurons
cards.explanation: Voluntary control descends in the corticospinal tracts straight to the phrenic and intercostal motor neurons, bypassing the medullary rhythm generator, which is why a person can override breathing for a while yet cannot suppress it indefinitely. The cortex does not send fibers to lung stretch receptors, which are sensory endings. Exciting the pre-Botzinger complex would speed breathing rather than stop it. The diaphragm is skeletal muscle with somatic innervation, so no sympathetic pathway drives it.

cards.q: Cold air and smoke stimulate irritant receptors in the airway lining. Predict the reflex response.
cards.a: Bronchoconstriction with coughing and rapid shallow breathing.
options: Bronchodilation with slow deep breathing
Bronchoconstriction with coughing and rapid shallow breathing
A long pause in breathing followed by a single deep breath
A rise in tidal volume with no change in airway diameter
cards.explanation: Irritant receptors act through vagal afferents to narrow the airways and produce cough and fast shallow breaths, which limits how deeply the irritant is drawn in. Bronchodilation with deep breathing would draw more of the irritant into the lung, the opposite of a protective reflex. A pause followed by a deep breath describes the sigh or the response after inflation, not irritation. Leaving airway diameter unchanged ignores the bronchoconstriction that defines this reflex.

cards.q: A patient has a complete spinal cord transection at C2. Trace the consequence for the diaphragm and for the medullary rhythm.
cards.a: The medulla still makes a rhythm but it cannot reach the phrenic motor neurons, so the diaphragm is paralyzed.
options: The medulla stops generating a rhythm of its own, so the diaphragm and the intercostal muscles both fall silent
The medulla still makes a rhythm but it cannot reach the phrenic motor neurons, so the diaphragm is paralyzed
The rhythm reaches the diaphragm normally, and only the intercostal and abdominal muscles are lost
The diaphragm keeps working because the phrenic nerve leaves the brainstem above the level of the injury
cards.explanation: The rhythm is made in the medulla, which is above the lesion and unaffected, but the descending pathway to the phrenic motor neurons at C3 through C5 is cut, so the command never arrives and ventilation fails without support. Saying the medulla stops firing confuses the site of rhythm generation with the site of injury. Losing only the intercostals describes a lower cervical or thoracic lesion. The phrenic nerve is a spinal nerve, not a cranial nerve, so it cannot bypass the cord.

cards.q: In an animal study, the brainstem is cut across the middle of the pons, separating the upper pons from the lower pons, and both vagus nerves are then cut. Predict the resulting pattern.
cards.a: Prolonged inspiratory holds interrupted by brief expirations.
options: Rapid shallow breathing at about twice the normal rate
A normal pattern, because the medulla alone is sufficient
Prolonged inspiratory holds interrupted by brief expirations
Complete and permanent apnea
cards.explanation: Two independent inspiratory off switches exist, the pneumotaxic center in the upper pons and the vagal stretch reflex, and this preparation removes both, leaving the apneustic drive of the lower pons unopposed so inspiration is held for long stretches. Rapid shallow breathing would follow from too much off switch activity, not too little. The pattern is not normal, because the medulla alone gives a rhythm but not normal inspiratory timing. Apnea does not occur, since the pre-Botzinger complex in the medulla is untouched.

cards.q: A child breathes normally while awake but hypoventilates badly during sleep, and arterial PCO2 climbs each night. Which explanation fits best?
cards.a: The automatic brainstem drive is impaired while the cortical pathway is intact.
options: The phrenic nerves conduct normally while awake but stop conducting during sleep
The automatic brainstem drive is impaired while the cortical pathway is intact
The voluntary cortical pathway is lost while the automatic brainstem drive is intact
The lung stretch receptors stop firing during sleep, which stalls each inspiration
cards.explanation: Automatic and voluntary control travel by separate routes, so a damaged brainstem drive can be masked while the child is awake and using cortical output, then unmasked as soon as sleep removes that cortical contribution. Losing the voluntary pathway would show up during deliberate breathing tasks, not during sleep. Nerve conduction does not switch off with sleep state. Stretch receptors shorten inspiration rather than sustain breathing, so silencing them would lengthen breaths, not stop them.

cards.q: A patient in pulmonary edema breathes rapidly and shallowly even though arterial PCO2 is low. Which receptors best account for the pattern?
cards.a: Juxtacapillary J receptors in the alveolar walls.
options: Slowly adapting stretch receptors in the airway smooth muscle
Juxtacapillary J receptors in the alveolar walls
Carotid body chemoreceptors responding to arterial H+
Central chemoreceptors in the medulla
cards.explanation: J receptors sit next to the pulmonary capillaries and fire when the interstitium swells with fluid, producing the rapid shallow breathing seen in edema, and they explain why ventilation is high while PCO2 is low. Central chemoreceptors would be inhibited, not excited, by a low PCO2, so they cannot be the driver here. Stretch receptors act to shorten inspiration during large breaths, and these breaths are small. Carotid bodies respond to acidosis, but blowing off CO2 has made the blood alkalotic.

cards.q: Where are the central chemoreceptors located?
cards.a: On the ventral surface of the medulla.
options: On the ventral surface of the medulla
In the carotid bodies at the fork of the common carotid artery
In the upper pons beside the pneumotaxic center
In the wall of the aortic arch
cards.explanation: The central chemoreceptors lie in the medulla near its ventral surface, bathed in brain extracellular fluid and cerebrospinal fluid, which is the compartment whose acidity they read. The carotid bodies and aortic arch bodies are the peripheral chemoreceptors, sitting in arterial blood instead. The pons contains centers that time breathing, not chemoreceptors, so naming it confuses the rhythm circuitry with the chemical sensors.

cards.q: What do the central chemoreceptors sense directly?
cards.a: H+ concentration in the brain extracellular fluid.
options: Arterial PO2 delivered to the medulla
H+ concentration in the arterial blood arriving at the medulla
Arterial PCO2 delivered to the medulla
H+ concentration in the brain extracellular fluid
cards.explanation: Central chemoreceptors respond to H+ in the fluid around them, and that H+ is produced locally when CO2 crosses into the brain and is hydrated to carbonic acid. They do not read arterial PCO2 itself, even though arterial PCO2 is what sets the amount of CO2 crossing over. They cannot read arterial H+ either, because H+ does not cross the blood brain barrier. Arterial PO2 is the business of the peripheral chemoreceptors, not the central ones.

cards.q: Which of these crosses the blood brain barrier easily?
cards.a: CO2.
options: HCO3-
CO2
Na+
H+
cards.explanation: CO2 is a small uncharged lipid soluble molecule, so it diffuses across the blood brain barrier freely and then generates H+ inside the brain fluid. H+ and HCO3- are charged and cross only slowly through transporters, which is why an arterial acid load does not immediately change central chemoreceptor firing. Na+ is likewise charged and tightly regulated at the barrier rather than free to diffuse.

cards.q: Where are the peripheral chemoreceptors found?
cards.a: In the carotid bodies and the aortic bodies.
options: In the carotid bodies and the aortic bodies
In the medullary reticular formation and the pons
In the alveolar walls and the airway smooth muscle
In the pulmonary arteries and the pulmonary veins
cards.explanation: The carotid bodies sit at the fork of each common carotid artery and the aortic bodies sit on the aortic arch, both places where they sample arterial blood just as it leaves for the brain and body. The medulla and pons hold the central chemoreceptors and the rhythm centers. Alveolar walls and airway smooth muscle hold J receptors and stretch receptors, which are mechanical sensors. The pulmonary vessels carry blood to be oxygenated and are not chemoreceptor sites.

cards.q: Which receptors respond to a large fall in arterial PO2?
cards.a: The peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies.
options: The central chemoreceptors on the ventral surface of the medulla
The peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies
The slowly adapting stretch receptors in the airway walls
The irritant receptors in the airway epithelial lining
cards.explanation: Only the peripheral chemoreceptors sense oxygen, and they increase their firing sharply when arterial PO2 drops well below normal. The central chemoreceptors are blind to oxygen and respond to H+ generated from CO2 in the brain fluid, so a low PO2 does not excite them. Stretch receptors report lung inflation and irritant receptors report chemical or particulate irritation of the airway, so neither reads blood gas levels.

cards.q: Which nerve carries carotid body signals to the medulla?
cards.a: The glossopharyngeal nerve.
options: The hypoglossal nerve
The vagus nerve
The phrenic nerve
The glossopharyngeal nerve
cards.explanation: Carotid body afferents run in the glossopharyngeal nerve to the nucleus of the solitary tract in the medulla. The vagus nerve is the right answer for the aortic bodies and for lung stretch receptors, so it is the easiest option to confuse with the key. The phrenic nerve is motor to the diaphragm and the hypoglossal nerve supplies tongue muscles, so neither carries chemoreceptor information.

cards.q: What is the normal arterial PCO2 in a healthy adult at rest?
cards.a: 40 mmHg.
options: 100 mmHg
24 mmHg
40 mmHg
60 mmHg
cards.explanation: Arterial PCO2 is held near 40 mmHg, and ventilation is adjusted minute to minute to defend that value. The figure 24 is close to the normal plasma bicarbonate in mEq/L, a different quantity that students often swap in. A PCO2 of 60 mmHg indicates significant hypoventilation. The value 100 mmHg is normal arterial PO2, not PCO2.

cards.q: Below roughly what arterial PO2 does the hypoxic drive to breathe become strong?
cards.a: About 60 mmHg.
options: About 20 mmHg
About 95 mmHg
About 80 mmHg
About 60 mmHg
cards.explanation: Peripheral chemoreceptor firing increases only modestly until arterial PO2 falls to about 60 mmHg, then rises steeply, which parallels the shoulder of the oxygen hemoglobin dissociation curve where saturation starts to drop fast. Values of 95 and 80 mmHg sit on the flat upper part of that curve, where saturation is still high and the drive is weak. Waiting until 20 mmHg would be far too late, since consciousness is usually lost before that.

cards.q: Arterial PCO2 rises from 40 to 45 mmHg in a healthy person. Which receptor group produces most of the resulting increase in ventilation?
cards.a: The central chemoreceptors.
options: The peripheral chemoreceptors
The lung stretch receptors
The two chemoreceptor groups contribute equally
The central chemoreceptors
cards.explanation: About 70 percent of the ventilatory response to a rise in CO2 comes from the central chemoreceptors, because the extra CO2 crosses into the brain fluid and drives H+ up there. The peripheral chemoreceptors do respond to CO2 as well, and they respond faster, but they supply the smaller share of the steady response. Stretch receptors have no chemical sensitivity at all. An equal split understates how much of the CO2 response is central.

cards.q: Why does a rise in arterial PCO2 lower cerebrospinal fluid pH more than it lowers arterial blood pH?
cards.a: Cerebrospinal fluid has very little protein buffer.
options: Cerebrospinal fluid has a higher starting bicarbonate concentration
Cerebrospinal fluid has very little protein buffer
Cerebrospinal fluid lacks carbonic anhydrase, so CO2 accumulates
Cerebrospinal fluid receives H+ directly from arterial blood
cards.explanation: Blood carries hemoglobin and plasma proteins that soak up H+, while cerebrospinal fluid is nearly protein free, so the same rise in CO2 produces a bigger pH swing there and the central chemoreceptors get a strong signal. Cerebrospinal fluid bicarbonate is not higher than plasma bicarbonate in a way that would explain this. Carbonic anhydrase is present in the surrounding cells, and its absence would blunt the response rather than sharpen it. H+ cannot move directly from blood into cerebrospinal fluid, which is exactly why the CO2 route matters.

cards.q: A person with carbon monoxide poisoning has a normal arterial PO2 but a badly reduced oxygen content. Predict the peripheral chemoreceptor response.
cards.a: Firing is nearly unchanged, because they sense dissolved oxygen.
options: Firing is nearly unchanged, because they sense dissolved oxygen
Firing rises sharply, because hemoglobin saturation has fallen
Firing rises sharply, because total oxygen delivery has fallen
Firing falls, because carbon monoxide directly inhibits the glomus cells
cards.explanation: Carotid and aortic body cells respond to the partial pressure of oxygen dissolved in plasma, and carbon monoxide poisoning leaves that partial pressure normal while ruining the amount carried on hemoglobin, so ventilation does not rise the way the tissue oxygen shortage would seem to demand. Answers based on total delivery or on saturation describe the real danger of the poisoning but not what the sensor measures. Carbon monoxide does not act as a direct inhibitor of the receptor, so a fall in firing is not the mechanism.

cards.q: In diabetic ketoacidosis, arterial H+ is high but cerebrospinal fluid pH has barely moved. Which receptors drive the deep rapid breathing?
cards.a: The peripheral chemoreceptors, since H+ cannot cross the blood brain barrier.
options: The lung stretch receptors, which respond to the larger tidal volumes
The pontine respiratory group, which is excited by circulating ketone bodies
The central chemoreceptors, which sense the arterial acid load directly
The peripheral chemoreceptors, since H+ cannot cross the blood brain barrier
cards.explanation: The carotid bodies sit in arterial blood and respond to arterial H+ within seconds, while the central chemoreceptors are shielded because H+ cannot cross the blood brain barrier, so at the start of a metabolic acidosis the drive is almost entirely peripheral. The central receptors join in later, once the falling PCO2 and slow bicarbonate shifts change brain fluid pH. Stretch receptors respond to the large breaths but do not cause them, and the pontine group has no chemical sensitivity.

cards.q: A healthy person at rest switches from room air to 100 percent oxygen. Predict the change in ventilation.
cards.a: Almost no change, because CO2 and not oxygen is the resting drive.
options: A large decrease, because the hypoxic drive is removed
Almost no change, because CO2 and not oxygen is the resting drive
An increase in rate with a matching fall in tidal volume
A large increase, because more oxygen reaches the chemoreceptors
cards.explanation: At a normal arterial PO2 of about 100 mmHg the peripheral chemoreceptors are contributing very little, so raising PO2 further removes almost nothing and ventilation is essentially unchanged apart from a small transient dip. A large decrease is what you would see in someone whose ventilation had come to depend on hypoxia, such as a chronic CO2 retainer, so that option is right under different conditions. Extra oxygen does not excite any receptor, and there is no mechanism to trade rate against depth here.

cards.q: Ventilation rises by roughly 2 L/min for each 1 mmHg rise in arterial PCO2. If resting ventilation is 6 L/min and PCO2 goes from 40 to 43 mmHg, what is the new ventilation?
cards.a: About 12 L/min.
options: About 12 L/min
About 18 L/min
About 24 L/min
About 8 L/min
cards.explanation: A 3 mmHg rise at 2 L/min per mmHg adds 6 L/min to the starting 6 L/min, giving about 12 L/min, and this steepness is why arterial PCO2 normally stays within a mmHg or two. About 8 L/min would follow from adding only 2 L/min total instead of 2 per mmHg. About 18 comes from adding 2 L/min per mmHg to a starting value of 12, and 24 comes from multiplying rather than adding. The point of the number is how small a CO2 change it takes to double ventilation.

cards.q: Which of these changes would raise ventilation the most in a healthy person?
cards.a: A rise in arterial PCO2 from 40 to 45 mmHg.
options: A rise in arterial PCO2 from 40 to 45 mmHg
A rise in arterial PO2 from 100 to 300 mmHg
A fall in arterial PCO2 from 40 to 37 mmHg
A fall in arterial PO2 from 100 to 85 mmHg
cards.explanation: A 5 mmHg rise in PCO2 roughly doubles ventilation, which is why CO2 is called the minute to minute drive to breathe. Dropping PO2 from 100 to 85 mmHg stays on the flat part of the oxygen curve and barely moves the peripheral chemoreceptors, so the ventilatory effect is small. Raising PO2 above normal does nothing, since the receptors are already quiet. Lowering PCO2 reduces the drive and would decrease ventilation, not raise it.

cards.q: A patient with long standing lung disease has held an arterial PCO2 near 60 mmHg for years, and cerebrospinal fluid pH has returned to normal. Which statement best explains that normal cerebrospinal fluid pH?
cards.a: Bicarbonate has been moved into the cerebrospinal fluid, buffering the extra H+.
options: The kidneys have lowered the arterial PCO2 back toward its normal 40 mmHg
Bicarbonate has been moved into the cerebrospinal fluid, buffering the extra H+
CO2 has stopped crossing the blood brain barrier at high concentrations
The central chemoreceptors have been permanently destroyed by the chronic acid load
cards.explanation: Over hours to days bicarbonate is moved into the cerebrospinal fluid, which restores its pH toward normal even while PCO2 stays high, so the central chemoreceptors quiet down and the CO2 drive is blunted. CO2 continues to cross the barrier freely at any concentration, so the transport step is not what changed. The receptors are adapted rather than destroyed, and their response returns if PCO2 climbs further. The kidneys adjust bicarbonate, not PCO2, which is set by ventilation.

cards.q: In an experiment the fluid bathing the medulla is perfused so its pH is held constant while arterial PCO2 is raised from 40 to 50 mmHg. Predict the central chemoreceptor response.
cards.a: Little or no increase in firing, because the H+ signal was prevented.
options: An increase in firing only if arterial PO2 also falls
A large increase in firing, because arterial PCO2 is the stimulus
Little or no increase in firing, because the H+ signal was prevented
A large decrease in firing, because the perfusion washes out CO2
cards.explanation: Clamping the pH of the brain fluid removes the H+ rise that CO2 would normally cause there, and the receptors go quiet, which is the classic demonstration that H+ and not CO2 itself is the stimulus. Expecting a large increase treats arterial PCO2 as the direct signal, which is the most common misreading of this pathway. The perfusion holds pH steady rather than stripping CO2, so a fall in firing is not expected. Central chemoreceptors do not respond to oxygen at all, so tying the answer to PO2 misassigns the peripheral role.

cards.q: Both carotid bodies are surgically removed in an experimental animal, and the aortic contribution is small. Predict the responses to acute hypoxia and to a rise in PCO2.
cards.a: The hypoxic response is nearly abolished while most of the CO2 response remains.
options: The hypoxic response is nearly abolished while most of the CO2 response remains
Both responses are preserved because the central chemoreceptors cover both stimuli
Both responses are nearly abolished
The CO2 response is nearly abolished while the hypoxic response remains
cards.explanation: The peripheral chemoreceptors are the only oxygen sensors, so removing them takes away the hypoxic drive, while the CO2 response survives largely intact because roughly 70 percent of it is central. Saying both responses are lost forgets that the medullary receptors are untouched. Losing the CO2 response and keeping the hypoxic one reverses the two roles. Central chemoreceptors cannot cover hypoxia, so no compensation restores that arm.

cards.q: Two subjects breathe a low oxygen mixture that brings arterial PO2 to 50 mmHg. In one, arterial PCO2 is held at 40 mmHg by adding CO2 to the mixture; in the other, PCO2 is allowed to fall as ventilation rises. Which subject ventilates more?
cards.a: The one whose PCO2 is held at 40 mmHg.
options: Neither increases ventilation, because PO2 is still above 40 mmHg
The one whose PCO2 is allowed to fall
The one whose PCO2 is held at 40 mmHg
Both the same, because the hypoxic stimulus is identical
cards.explanation: Hypoxia drives ventilation up, but in the second subject the extra breathing blows off CO2, and the falling PCO2 removes central drive and brakes the response, so holding PCO2 at 40 lets the full hypoxic response show. Assuming the two are equal ignores that the two stimuli interact rather than acting alone. Expecting no response at all misses that 50 mmHg is well below the 60 mmHg point where the hypoxic drive becomes strong.

cards.q: What happens to ventilation in the first few seconds after exercise begins?
cards.a: It rises abruptly, before blood gases have changed.
options: It falls briefly and then rises once lactate appears
It stays at the resting level until oxygen consumption doubles
It rises abruptly, before blood gases have changed
It rises slowly over about two minutes as PCO2 climbs
cards.explanation: Ventilation jumps almost the instant movement starts, well before arterial blood has time to circulate and report any change, so the rise cannot be caused by a chemical signal. A slow rise driven by climbing PCO2 describes what students often assume but not what recordings show, and in moderate exercise PCO2 barely moves. Ventilation does not dip at the start, and it does not wait for lactate, which appears only in heavier work.

cards.q: What causes the abrupt jump in ventilation at the very start of exercise?
cards.a: Feedforward signals from the motor cortex and limb proprioceptors.
options: A sudden fall in arterial PO2 sensed by the carotid and aortic bodies
Feedforward signals from the motor cortex and limb proprioceptors
A sudden rise in the H+ concentration of the cerebrospinal fluid
Stretch receptor firing produced by the deeper breaths
cards.explanation: The motor cortex sends collateral signals to the respiratory centers as it commands the muscles, and moving joints and muscles add proprioceptive input, so breathing is turned up in anticipation rather than in response. Arterial PO2 does not fall in moderate exercise, so the carotid bodies have nothing new to report. Cerebrospinal fluid H+ changes too slowly to explain a response measured in seconds. Stretch receptors respond to the deeper breaths but do not initiate them.

cards.q: During moderate steady state exercise, what happens to arterial PCO2?
cards.a: It stays close to its resting value.
options: It stays close to its resting value
It rises for a minute and then climbs further as work continues
It rises steadily as muscle CO2 production climbs
It falls steadily because breathing increases first
cards.explanation: Ventilation increases in proportion to CO2 production, so the extra CO2 is cleared as fast as it is made and arterial PCO2 is held near 40 mmHg, which is one of the most striking pieces of matching in the whole system. A steady rise would mean ventilation was lagging behind metabolism, which happens only in disease or very heavy work. A steady fall is seen above the lactate threshold in heavy exercise, so that answer is correct under different conditions.

cards.q: As exercise intensity increases from rest, which changes first and more?
cards.a: Tidal volume increases before breathing rate does.
options: Both increase together in exact proportion throughout
Neither changes until oxygen consumption has tripled
Breathing rate increases before tidal volume does
Tidal volume increases before breathing rate does
cards.explanation: Deepening each breath is the more efficient way to raise ventilation, because dead space is a fixed volume and larger breaths waste a smaller fraction of each one, so tidal volume climbs first and rate rises later as work becomes heavy. Leading with rate would move more air through dead space for the same effort. The two do not scale in exact proportion, and ventilation begins rising within seconds of the first movement, not after oxygen use has tripled.

cards.q: Compared with sea level, what is different about the air at 4000 m?
cards.a: Barometric pressure is lower while the fraction of oxygen is unchanged.
options: Barometric pressure is lower and the fraction of oxygen is higher
The fraction of oxygen is lower while barometric pressure is unchanged
Both barometric pressure and the fraction of oxygen are lower
Barometric pressure is lower while the fraction of oxygen is unchanged
cards.explanation: Air is well mixed, so oxygen makes up about 21 percent of it at any altitude, and what falls with height is the total pressure, which drags the partial pressure of oxygen down with it. Saying the fraction falls is the most common version of this misconception and would predict the same problem even in a pressurized cabin. Neither the fraction falling as well nor the fraction rising matches how the atmosphere is composed.

cards.q: What acid base disturbance appears in the first hours at high altitude?
cards.a: Respiratory alkalosis.
options: Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis
Respiratory acidosis
cards.explanation: Hypoxia drives hyperventilation, which blows off CO2 and raises pH, so the primary problem is respiratory and the direction is alkaline. Respiratory acidosis would require CO2 to be retained, which is the opposite of what hyperventilation does. Both metabolic answers describe a primary change in bicarbonate or fixed acid, whereas the first event at altitude is a change in breathing.

cards.q: Which hormone rises during altitude acclimatization to increase red blood cell production?
cards.a: Erythropoietin.
options: Atrial natriuretic peptide
Aldosterone
Antidiuretic hormone
Erythropoietin
cards.explanation: Kidney cells sense low oxygen and release erythropoietin, which stimulates the bone marrow so that hematocrit and oxygen carrying capacity climb over the following weeks. Aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone regulate sodium and water handling, so they change blood volume rather than red cell number. Atrial natriuretic peptide promotes sodium and water loss and has no role in red cell production.

cards.q: Which organ compensates for the respiratory alkalosis of altitude?
cards.a: The kidney, by excreting bicarbonate.
options: The lung, by retaining CO2
The liver, by producing more plasma protein buffer
The spleen, by releasing stored red cells
The kidney, by excreting bicarbonate
cards.explanation: The kidney pulls plasma pH back toward normal over a day or two by dumping bicarbonate in the urine, which also releases the brake that alkalosis had placed on ventilation. Having the lung retain CO2 would undo the hyperventilation that is protecting oxygenation. Liver protein synthesis is far too slow and too small to correct a pH shift, and the spleen affects red cell number rather than acid base balance.

cards.q: At an altitude where barometric pressure is 380 mmHg, what is the partial pressure of oxygen in warmed humidified inspired air? Water vapor pressure is 47 mmHg and oxygen is 21 percent of dry air.
cards.a: About 70 mmHg.
options: About 100 mmHg
About 50 mmHg
About 70 mmHg
About 80 mmHg
cards.explanation: Subtract the water vapor first, since airway gas is fully humidified, giving 380 minus 47 equals 333 mmHg of dry gas, and 21 percent of that is about 70 mmHg. About 100 mmHg is the sea level value for this calculation and shows the size of the altitude penalty. About 80 mmHg comes from taking 21 percent of 380 without removing water vapor. About 50 mmHg is closer to a normal venous PO2 and does not come from this computation.

cards.q: Above the lactate threshold, ventilation climbs more steeply than oxygen consumption does. What best explains the extra ventilation?
cards.a: Bicarbonate buffering of lactic acid releases additional CO2.
options: The Hering-Breuer reflex is recruited by the deeper breaths
Bicarbonate buffering of lactic acid releases additional CO2
Arterial PO2 falls below 60 mmHg and adds a hypoxic drive
Lactate itself binds to the central chemoreceptors
cards.explanation: Lactic acid is buffered by bicarbonate, and that reaction generates CO2 over and above what the mitochondria are producing, so ventilation rises out of proportion to oxygen use and arterial PCO2 may even start to fall. Arterial PO2 stays near normal in healthy people even in heavy exercise, so hypoxia is not the trigger. Lactate does not reach the central chemoreceptors, since it is charged and does not cross the blood brain barrier. The Hering-Breuer reflex shortens inspiration and would limit ventilation rather than increase it.

cards.q: On the first day at 4000 m a climber hyperventilates, but ventilation does not rise as far as the hypoxia alone would predict. Why?
cards.a: The falling PCO2 and rising pH reduce the central chemoreceptor drive.
options: Airway stretch receptors cap the tidal volume that can be reached
Erythropoietin has not yet raised the hematocrit
The carotid bodies adapt within minutes and stop firing
The falling PCO2 and rising pH reduce the central chemoreceptor drive
cards.explanation: Hyperventilation blows off CO2, so brain fluid H+ falls and the central chemoreceptors pull back, opposing the peripheral drive from hypoxia and holding ventilation short of its full potential. The carotid bodies do not shut off within minutes; their hypoxic firing persists and even increases over days. Stretch receptors limit individual breath size but do not set the overall level of ventilation. The rise in hematocrit takes weeks and is not what restrains breathing on day one.

cards.q: Red cell 2,3-BPG rises during acclimatization to altitude. Predict the effect on the oxygen hemoglobin dissociation curve and on the tissues.
cards.a: The curve shifts right, so more oxygen is unloaded in the tissues.
options: The curve shifts right, so more oxygen is unloaded in the tissues
The curve shifts right, so less oxygen is unloaded in the tissues
The curve does not shift, but total carrying capacity rises
The curve shifts left, so more oxygen is loaded in the lung
cards.explanation: 2,3-BPG binds hemoglobin and lowers its oxygen affinity, shifting the curve right so that at any given tissue PO2 more oxygen comes off the molecule. A right shift always means easier unloading, so pairing a right shift with less unloading contradicts the definition. A left shift would improve loading in the lung but make delivery to tissue harder, and it is not what 2,3-BPG does. Carrying capacity is set by hemoglobin amount, a separate acclimatization change.

cards.q: After several weeks at altitude, hematocrit rises from 45 to 58 percent. Predict the paired consequences.
cards.a: Oxygen carrying capacity rises and blood viscosity rises.
options: Oxygen carrying capacity rises and blood viscosity falls
Oxygen carrying capacity falls and blood viscosity rises
Oxygen carrying capacity rises and blood viscosity rises
Oxygen carrying capacity is unchanged and blood viscosity rises
cards.explanation: More red cells means more hemoglobin per unit of blood, which raises how much oxygen the blood can carry, but the same crowding thickens the blood so the heart must work harder to move it. This is why altitude polycythemia is a trade rather than a pure gain. Viscosity cannot fall when cell concentration rises, and carrying capacity cannot fall or stay flat when hemoglobin per unit volume increases.

cards.q: When exercise stops, ventilation drops sharply within a few seconds and then declines slowly over minutes. What explains the sharp initial drop?
cards.a: Loss of the feedforward and proprioceptive input from the muscles.
options: An immediate fall in body temperature back to its baseline value
Rapid clearance of lactate from the blood by the liver and heart
Loss of the feedforward and proprioceptive input from the muscles
An immediate return of arterial PCO2 to its normal resting value
cards.explanation: The neural signals that turned breathing up switch off the moment movement stops, producing the abrupt fall, while the slower decline reflects the time needed to clear the CO2, acid and heat that the exercise generated. Arterial PCO2 does not snap back instantly, since the stored CO2 has to be blown off. Body temperature falls over many minutes, so it belongs to the slow phase. Lactate clearance also takes many minutes and cannot explain a change measured in seconds.

cards.q: A sea level resident has been at 4000 m for three days. Compared with the first hour after arrival, what has happened to ventilation, arterial pH, and urine bicarbonate?
cards.a: Ventilation is higher, arterial pH is closer to normal, and urine bicarbonate is increased.
options: Ventilation is higher, arterial pH is closer to normal, and urine bicarbonate is increased
Ventilation is unchanged, arterial pH is more alkaline, and urine bicarbonate is increased
Ventilation is higher, arterial pH is more acidic than normal, and urine bicarbonate is decreased
Ventilation is lower, arterial pH is more alkaline, and urine bicarbonate is decreased
cards.explanation: The kidney has been dumping bicarbonate for a couple of days, so the alkalosis is largely corrected, and with pH back near normal the central brake on breathing is released and ventilation climbs above its day one level. Falling ventilation would mean the hypoxia had resolved, which it has not. Persisting alkalosis with high urine bicarbonate is internally inconsistent, since excreting bicarbonate is exactly what corrects the pH. Arterial pH does not overshoot into acidosis, because renal compensation corrects toward normal rather than past it.

cards.q: Two climbers stand together at 4500 m. One arrived an hour ago from sea level, the other has lived there for a month. Compare their ventilation and their arterial pH.
cards.a: The long term resident ventilates more and has a pH nearer normal.
options: The long term resident ventilates more and has a pH nearer normal
Both ventilate the same, since the inspired PO2 is identical
The long term resident ventilates less and is more alkalotic
The newcomer ventilates more and has a pH nearer normal
cards.explanation: The newcomer is held back by the acute hypocapnic alkalosis, while the resident has excreted bicarbonate in blood and adjusted it in the cerebrospinal fluid, so the central brake is gone and ventilation can match the hypoxic stimulus. Saying the newcomer ventilates more reverses the time course of acclimatization. Equal ventilation ignores that the same inspired PO2 produces different responses depending on how much renal and cerebrospinal adjustment has occurred. The resident is less alkalotic, not more, because the compensation has happened.

cards.q: A runner in heavy exercise has arterial PO2 of 98 mmHg, PCO2 of 36 mmHg, and pH of 7.32, yet ventilation is five times resting. Which stimulus best accounts for the high ventilation?
cards.a: Neural drive from the exercising muscles plus acid at the carotid bodies.
options: The high arterial PCO2 acting on the central chemoreceptors in the medulla
Neural drive from the exercising muscles plus acid at the carotid bodies
Lung stretch receptor firing that drives the breathing rate upward
The low arterial PO2 acting on the peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid bodies
cards.explanation: Arterial PO2 is normal and PCO2 is actually below resting, so neither of the usual chemical explanations works, and what is left is the exercise feedforward drive plus the acid from lactate stimulating the carotid bodies. Calling PO2 low misreads 98 mmHg, which is a normal value. Calling PCO2 high misreads 36 mmHg, which is lower than the resting 40 and would if anything restrain breathing. Stretch receptors respond to the deeper breaths but do not generate the drive.

cards.q: A person acclimatized to 4000 m for six months returns to sea level. Predict ventilation over the first days and hematocrit over the following weeks.
cards.a: Ventilation falls back toward normal within days and hematocrit falls over weeks.
options: Ventilation stays elevated for months and hematocrit falls within hours
Ventilation rises further for days and hematocrit rises over weeks
Ventilation falls back toward normal within days and hematocrit falls over weeks
Ventilation falls back toward normal within days while hematocrit stays elevated permanently
cards.explanation: The hypoxic stimulus disappears the moment inspired PO2 returns to sea level values, so the extra ventilatory drive fades quickly, and with tissue oxygen restored erythropoietin falls and the excess red cells are not replaced as they age out over weeks. Ventilation cannot rise further with the stimulus removed. The elevated hematocrit is maintained only by continued hypoxia, so it is not permanent. Red cells live about 120 days, so hematocrit cannot drop within hours.

cards.q: What does one minute of voluntary hyperventilation do to arterial PCO2?
cards.a: It lowers it below 40 mmHg.
options: It raises it above 40 mmHg
It lowers it below 40 mmHg
It leaves it unchanged, since PCO2 is tightly defended
It raises it briefly and then lowers it below 40 mmHg
cards.explanation: Hyperventilation moves more air than metabolism requires, so CO2 is cleared from the alveoli faster than the blood delivers it and arterial PCO2 drops, often into the twenties. A rise would require moving less air, not more. PCO2 is defended by the reflex system, but voluntary cortical drive overrides that defense, which is the whole point of the maneuver. There is no initial rise, because clearance increases from the very first deep breath.

cards.q: What breathing pattern is expected immediately after a bout of voluntary hyperventilation?
cards.a: A period of apnea or clearly reduced breathing.
options: A single very deep breath followed by normal breathing
A period of apnea or clearly reduced breathing
A period of even faster and deeper breathing
Breathing that returns instantly to the resting pattern
cards.explanation: PCO2 has been driven below the threshold that normally keeps the respiratory centers firing, so once the voluntary effort stops there is little chemical drive and breathing pauses or becomes shallow until CO2 rebuilds. Faster breathing would require more drive, not less. An instant return to the resting pattern would only happen if PCO2 had not changed. A single deep breath is the pattern of a sigh, not of recovery from hypocapnia.

cards.q: During rebreathing from a closed bag, what happens to the gas in the bag?
cards.a: CO2 rises and oxygen falls.
options: CO2 rises while oxygen stays constant
CO2 falls and oxygen rises
CO2 and oxygen both rise
CO2 rises and oxygen falls
cards.explanation: The subject keeps consuming oxygen from the bag and keeps adding CO2 to it, and because the bag is closed neither change can be washed out, so the two gases move in opposite directions. CO2 falling would require fresh air entering the system. Both gases cannot rise, since the total volume is fixed and one is being consumed. Oxygen cannot stay constant while metabolism continues to draw on it.

cards.q: During a voluntary breath hold, what happens to arterial PCO2?
cards.a: It rises steadily.
options: It stays constant until oxygen is exhausted
It falls at first and then rises
It falls steadily
It rises steadily
cards.explanation: Metabolism keeps delivering CO2 to the blood while no air is being moved, so CO2 accumulates and arterial PCO2 climbs about 3 to 6 mmHg in the first minute. A fall would require ventilation, which is exactly what has been stopped. PCO2 does not wait for oxygen to run out, since CO2 production and O2 consumption go on together from the first second of the hold.

cards.q: In a normal subject, what mainly produces the breakpoint that ends a breath hold?
cards.a: The rising PCO2 and H+ concentration.
options: The loss of firing from the lung stretch receptors
The falling arterial PO2
The rising PCO2 and H+ concentration
The collapse of the alveoli during the hold
cards.explanation: CO2 accumulates quickly and the chemoreceptors are steeply sensitive to it, so the urge to breathe becomes irresistible while oxygen stores are still adequate. The falling PO2 contributes toward the end of a long hold but is not what sets the breakpoint in a normal breath hold, since PO2 usually stays above the level where hypoxic drive is strong. Alveoli do not collapse during a held breath at normal lung volume, and stretch receptor firing shortens inspiration rather than driving the urge to breathe.

cards.q: In the ventilation lab, which measurement represents the depth of breathing?
cards.a: Tidal volume.
options: Breathing frequency
Vital capacity
Tidal volume
Minute ventilation
cards.explanation: Tidal volume is the amount of air moved in a single ordinary breath, which is precisely what depth means on a spirogram. Frequency counts how many breaths occur per minute and is the other factor being recorded. Vital capacity is the largest possible single breath, a maximal test rather than a measure of resting depth. Minute ventilation is the product of depth and frequency, so it mixes both variables together.

cards.q: What is the effect of hyperventilating just before a breath hold?
cards.a: The breath hold lasts longer.
options: The breath hold lasts longer
The breath hold is unchanged in length
The breath hold ends immediately with a strong urge to breathe
The breath hold is shorter
cards.explanation: Starting from a low PCO2 means more time passes before CO2 climbs back to the level that triggers the breakpoint, so the hold is measurably longer. A shorter hold is what follows exercise, which raises CO2 production and starts the subject closer to the threshold. No change would only be expected if the maneuver had failed to lower PCO2. The urge to breathe is delayed rather than immediate, which is exactly what makes this maneuver hazardous before underwater swimming.

cards.q: What is the effect of a minute of vigorous exercise just before a breath hold?
cards.a: The breath hold is shorter.
options: The breath hold is longer only if the subject also hyperventilates
The breath hold is longer
The breath hold is shorter
The breath hold is unchanged in length
cards.explanation: Exercise raises CO2 production, so during the hold arterial PCO2 climbs faster and reaches the breakpoint sooner. A longer hold would require slowing CO2 accumulation, which exercise does the opposite of. Saying there is no change ignores that CO2 production is the variable that sets how fast the drive builds. Hyperventilation does lengthen a hold, but the question asks about exercise on its own, and its effect is a shorter hold.

cards.q: A student feels lightheaded with tingling fingers after hyperventilating in lab. What explains those symptoms?
cards.a: Low PCO2 causes cerebral vasoconstriction and alkalosis.
options: Low PCO2 causes cerebral vasoconstriction and alkalosis
High PCO2 causes cerebral vasodilation and acidosis
Low arterial PO2 starves the brain of oxygen
High arterial PO2 causes oxygen toxicity in the nerves
cards.explanation: CO2 is a powerful cerebral vasodilator, so blowing it off narrows brain vessels and reduces cerebral blood flow, which produces the lightheadedness, while the alkalosis increases nerve excitability and causes the tingling. High PCO2 would dilate rather than constrict and is the opposite of what hyperventilation produces. Arterial PO2 actually rises slightly during hyperventilation, so hypoxia is not the cause, and the small rise in PO2 from breathing room air is nowhere near toxic.

cards.q: During rebreathing from a bag, a student's tidal volume climbs from 500 to 900 mL and rate from 12 to 20 breaths per minute. Which change in the bag gas explains most of this?
cards.a: The rising CO2 concentration.
options: The falling oxygen concentration
The rising CO2 concentration
The rising water vapor content of the bag
The rising temperature of the bag gas
cards.explanation: Ventilation is steeply sensitive to CO2, so the accumulating CO2 in the bag drives both depth and rate up long before oxygen has fallen far enough to matter. Oxygen does fall during rebreathing, but it must drop below about 60 mmHg before the peripheral chemoreceptors add much, so it contributes only late in the trial. Water vapor and temperature both rise in the bag, but there are no receptors that convert either into a ventilatory drive.

cards.q: Two students have the same minute ventilation. One breathes 500 mL twelve times a minute, the other 250 mL twenty four times a minute. With 150 mL of dead space, which clears more CO2?
cards.a: The student taking 500 mL breaths.
options: The student taking 500 mL breaths
Neither clears CO2, because dead space exceeds tidal volume
The student taking 250 mL breaths
They clear CO2 equally, since minute ventilation is the same
cards.explanation: Alveolar ventilation is what clears CO2, and it equals tidal volume minus dead space times rate, so the deep pattern gives 350 times 12 or 4200 mL/min while the shallow pattern gives only 100 times 24 or 2400 mL/min. Equal minute ventilation is exactly the trap here, because dead space is wasted on every breath, so taking more breaths wastes more. Dead space does not exceed either tidal volume, so both patterns do ventilate alveoli, just unequally.

cards.q: A subject breathes 10 times a minute at 600 mL at rest, then 16 times a minute at 750 mL near the end of rebreathing. How much did minute ventilation increase?
cards.a: From 6 to 12 L/min.
options: From 6 to 15 L/min
From 6 to 18 L/min
From 6 to 9 L/min
From 6 to 12 L/min
cards.explanation: Minute ventilation is rate times tidal volume, so 10 times 600 is 6000 mL/min or 6 L/min, and 16 times 750 is 12000 mL/min or 12 L/min, a doubling produced by the rising CO2. About 9 L/min is what you get by letting the rate rise to 16 while holding tidal volume at the resting 600 mL, so it counts only half the change. The 15 and 18 L/min answers overshoot, and neither can be produced by pairing the rate and depth that were actually recorded.

cards.q: A student's breath hold goes from 40 seconds to 85 seconds after hyperventilating. Which variable did the maneuver change to produce that result?
cards.a: The starting arterial PCO2, which began much lower.
options: The oxygen stored in the lungs, which began much higher
The starting arterial PCO2, which began much lower
The sensitivity of the central chemoreceptors, which was reduced
The volume of the dead space, which was reduced
cards.explanation: Hyperventilation pushes PCO2 well below 40 mmHg, so during the hold it takes far longer for CO2 to climb back to the breakpoint threshold, and the hold roughly doubles. Lung oxygen stores rise only slightly with hyperventilation on room air and are not what limits a normal hold. Receptor sensitivity is a property of the tissue and does not change over a minute of deep breathing. Dead space is an anatomical volume and is unaffected by how hard someone breathes.

cards.q: After hyperventilation the subject shows 25 seconds of apnea. What ends the apnea?
cards.a: CO2 accumulates until the chemoreceptor threshold is reached again.
options: Oxygen stores fall low enough to excite the carotid bodies
The lung stretch receptors stop firing at low lung volume
CO2 accumulates until the chemoreceptor threshold is reached again
The cortex takes over and forces a voluntary breath
cards.explanation: Metabolism keeps producing CO2 during the pause, so PCO2 climbs back toward 40 mmHg and the chemoreceptors resume driving the respiratory centers, which restarts breathing without any conscious effort. Oxygen would take much longer than 25 seconds to fall to a level that excites the carotid bodies, so hypoxia is not the trigger here. Stretch receptors report inflation rather than initiate breaths. The apnea ends automatically, which is why the subject cannot prevent it by choosing not to breathe.

cards.q: Why does the urge to breathe during a normal breath hold appear well before oxygen stores become dangerously low?
cards.a: The CO2 threshold is reached first, because ventilation is far more sensitive to CO2.
options: The central chemoreceptors detect the falling oxygen before the tissues suffer
The CO2 threshold is reached first, because ventilation is far more sensitive to CO2
Oxygen falls faster than CO2 rises, so hypoxia arrives first
The lungs empty during the hold, which triggers the urge mechanically
cards.explanation: Ventilation responds strongly to a few mmHg of CO2 while it barely responds to oxygen until PO2 falls below about 60 mmHg, so the CO2 signal wins the race and provides an early warning. Oxygen does fall during a hold, but not fast enough to reach that threshold before the CO2 alarm sounds. The lungs stay inflated during a held breath, so no mechanical emptying occurs. Central chemoreceptors have no oxygen sensitivity, so they cannot supply an early hypoxia warning.

cards.q: Three traces are recorded. In trace A a burst of very deep rapid breaths is followed by a 20 second pause. In trace B rate and depth climb steadily for two minutes. In trace C the trace is flat for 45 seconds and then one large breath follows. Match the maneuvers.
cards.a: A is the recovery after hyperventilation, B is rebreathing, C is a breath hold.
options: A is the recovery after hyperventilation, B is rebreathing, C is a breath hold
A is the recovery after hyperventilation, B is a breath hold, C is rebreathing
A is a breath hold, B is the recovery after hyperventilation, C is rebreathing
A is rebreathing, B is a breath hold, C is the recovery after hyperventilation
cards.explanation: A pause that follows a burst of deep rapid breathing is the post hyperventilation apnea, produced by a PCO2 driven below the threshold that normally keeps the centers firing. A steady climb in both rate and depth over minutes is rebreathing, because bag CO2 keeps rising. A flat stretch followed by one large breath is a voluntary breath hold ending at the breakpoint. The other combinations misread the key feature, which is whether the pause was forced by a low CO2 or chosen by the subject.

cards.q: A swimmer hyperventilates hard, then swims underwater and loses consciousness without ever feeling a strong urge to breathe. Trace the sequence that explains this.
cards.a: Low starting PCO2 delayed the urge to breathe while exercise consumed oxygen, so PO2 fell too far.
options: Hyperventilation loaded the blood with so much extra oxygen that it masked the urge to breathe
Low starting PCO2 delayed the urge to breathe while exercise consumed oxygen, so PO2 fell too far
High starting PCO2 blunted the central chemoreceptors, so no signal to breathe was ever generated
Swimming stimulated lung stretch receptors that actively suppressed the urge to breathe
cards.explanation: The maneuver lowers PCO2 without meaningfully raising oxygen stores, so the CO2 alarm is postponed while swimming burns oxygen fast, and PO2 can reach the level that causes blackout before the breakpoint ever arrives. Hemoglobin is already about 98 percent saturated on room air, so hyperventilation cannot load much extra oxygen. Hyperventilation lowers PCO2 rather than raising it, so the high PCO2 explanation has the direction backward. Stretch receptors shorten inspiration and do not suppress the chemical drive.

cards.q: A subject rebreathes from a bag fitted with a CO2 absorber, so bag CO2 stays near zero while oxygen falls. Predict the ventilation trace.
cards.a: Ventilation changes little at first, then rises sharply once PO2 falls below 60 mmHg.
options: Ventilation stays flat throughout, because only CO2 is able to drive breathing
Ventilation rises steadily from the very first breath, just as in ordinary rebreathing
Ventilation changes little at first, then rises sharply once PO2 falls below 60 mmHg
Ventilation falls progressively as oxygen is steadily removed from the bag
cards.explanation: Removing the CO2 removes the main drive, so the early part of the trial is nearly silent, and the increase waits until arterial PO2 drops onto the steep part of the peripheral chemoreceptor response near 60 mmHg. A steady rise from the first breath is what happens without the absorber, when CO2 is free to accumulate. Ventilation does not fall, because hypoxia excites rather than inhibits the carotid bodies at these levels. It does not stay flat forever either, since the hypoxic drive eventually takes over.

cards.q: In a rebreathing trial, ventilation begins climbing when bag CO2 reaches about 45 mmHg, at a moment when bag PO2 is still 105 mmHg. What does this timing show?
cards.a: CO2 drives the response, since ventilation rose while oxygen was still normal.
options: Oxygen drives the response, since both gases were changing at once
Neither gas drives the response, since the change is caused by bag rebreathing itself
CO2 drives the response, since ventilation rose while oxygen was still normal
Both gases drive the response equally, since each moved from its starting value
cards.explanation: A PO2 of 105 mmHg is normal and leaves the peripheral chemoreceptors nearly silent, so the only stimulus that has changed enough to matter at that moment is the CO2, which is why ventilation tracks it. Attributing the rise to oxygen ignores that oxygen has not yet fallen anywhere near the 60 mmHg threshold. The act of rebreathing changes the gases but is not itself a stimulus. Calling the two equal ignores the very different sensitivities, which is exactly what this trial is designed to reveal.
